scenes.title: Two TLS legs across an ALB
scenes.visual_overview: This slide explains two tls legs across an alb by following the pictured security architecture.
visual_walkthrough: Identify the featured AWS service and the full context

On the left, the client negotiates TLS with the Application Load Balancer, which presents its configured listener certificate. That first TLS connection ends at the ALB. The upper-right path depicts an HTTPS target group: the ALB creates a new TLS connection to the backend target. The lower dashed path uses an HTTP target group, leaving that backend leg unencrypted. These are separate trust and transport boundaries; an encrypted front-end connection does not prove every hop is encrypted.
Distinguish permission, security and operational responsibilities
Use an HTTPS target group when the design requires backend transport encryption.

scenes.title: ALB mutual TLS modes
scenes.visual_overview: This slide explains alb mutual tls modes by following the pictured security architecture.
visual_walkthrough: Identify the featured AWS service and the full context

The left panel shows a client with its own certificate and private key. The ALB presents its server certificate and the client validates it; the client also presents its certificate. In verify mode, the ALB validates the client certificate against a configured trust store and optional supported revocation checks. In passthrough mode, ALB forwards certificate details in HTTP headers for the application to validate, instead of validating them itself. This is not raw TCP passthrough.
Distinguish permission, security and operational responsibilities
Client certificate authentication is separate from application-level authorization.

scenes.title: Certificate issue, renewal and revocation
scenes.visual_overview: This slide explains certificate issue, renewal and revocation by following the pictured security architecture.
visual_walkthrough: Identify the featured AWS service and the full context

Read the lifecycle ring clockwise. First, issue and deploy a certificate containing the right hostname, trust chain, endpoint and Region. Second, renew before expiration; maintain DNS validation records where required and replace imported certificates yourself. Third, revoke compromised or untrusted credentials using supported CRL or OCSP workflows and relevant trust-store changes. The lower troubleshooting strip checks hostname, chain, validity and endpoint deployment in that order. Not every service checks revocation the same way.
Distinguish permission, security and operational responsibilities
A valid certificate today needs ongoing monitoring, renewal, trust distribution and incident procedures.
